{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_ecee26d9-1caf-441a-a4e2-80b789337129","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_ecee26d9-1caf-441a-a4e2-80b789337129","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Billing Events Stream Runbook","body":"# Billing Events Stream Runbook

The `billing-events` stream carries one record per billing state change:
subscription created, plan moved, invoice settled, refund issued. Three services
produce to it and every finance-facing report consumes it, directly or through
the settled-invoice view.

## Tiering

`billing-events` is a **regulated-tier** stream. Regulated tier is not a
property of the payload, it is a property of what downstream consumers are
obliged to do with it, and it brings its own operating rules
(mcp:knowledge_page:kp_3ca1897f-da19-4659-9ca1-5dfecf17b34d). Those rules, not this runbook, decide how a
proposed change to the stream is announced and how long producers have to
prepare for it.

## Replay

The stream retains fourteen days of records and can be replayed from any offset
inside that window. A replay is visible to consumers as duplicate keys, so a
consumer that is not idempotent must be paused for the duration. The field
meanings and the enumerations each field accepts are documented in
mcp:knowledge_page:kp_1e4d735a-d16d-4468-b297-b61ff566e20b.

## Adding a producer

A new producer is onboarded through the standard stream checklist
(mcp:knowledge_page:kp_d17373be-a7c0-480c-b4d5-ab43f9870250); the checklist covers the mechanics, not
the notice a schema change owes its consumers.","references":[{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_1e4d735a-d16d-4468-b297-b61ff566e20b","type":"knowledge_page"},{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_3ca1897f-da19-4659-9ca1-5dfecf17b34d","type":"knowledge_page"},{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_d17373be-a7c0-480c-b4d5-ab43f9870250","type":"knowledge_page"}]}}

Every interface the platform publishes carries a change class. The class is what
decides the paperwork and the notice, so a change is planned from its class
rather than from its size.

## Classes

**CC-1 — local.** No published interface changes. The owning team signs it off
and no notice is owed.

**CC-2 — additive.** A compatible addition to a published interface. The owning
team signs it off and consumers are given two business days of advance notice.

**CC-3 — governed.** A change to an interface whose consumers carry an
obligation of their own. Sign-off is the governance group's, and consumers are
owed **9 business days of advance notice** before the change is applied.

**CC-4 — breaking.** A change that invalidates a published contract. Sign-off is
the governance group's, consumers are owed a full quarter of notice, and the old
contract runs in parallel until the last consumer has moved.

**CC-5 — emergency.** A change applied ahead of its notice because leaving the
defect in place is worse. Sign-off is the duty manager's and the notice is
reconstructed afterwards, with the reason recorded.

## Counting the notice

Notice is counted in business days from the announcement to the change window
opening, excluding the announcement day itself. A notice period that would end
inside a change freeze runs to the first business day after the freeze lifts.

Where an announcement goes out, and what it has to contain, is a channel
question rather than a class question (mcp:knowledge_page:kp_84131291-ec94-4399-8b06-1572353a474b).","references":[{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_84131291-ec94-4399-8b06-1572353a474b","type":"knowledge_page"}]}}

{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_3ca1897f-da19-4659-9ca1-5dfecf17b34d","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_3ca1897f-da19-4659-9ca1-5dfecf17b34d","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Regulated Tier Operating Rules","body":"# Regulated Tier Operating Rules

A stream enters the regulated tier when a downstream consumer is obliged to
reproduce its contents on demand. The tier is assigned by the data governance
group and reviewed annually.

## What the tier obliges

- **Retention floor.** A regulated stream keeps at least fourteen days of
  replayable records, regardless of the volume that implies.
- **Access review.** Every principal with read access is re-confirmed each
  quarter; an unconfirmed principal loses access at the review date rather than
  at a grace period after it.
- **Producer attestation.** Each producing service names an owner who attests,
  at onboarding and after any change, that the records it writes are complete.

## Changes

**Every regulated-tier stream is governed by change class CC-3.** The change
class fixes how a proposed change is announced, who signs it off and how much
advance notice consumers are owed; the classes are defined in
mcp:knowledge_page:kp_fb51a148-2fa5-4db6-a76b-217f70795075. A change that a stream owner believes needs
less notice than its class requires is a request to reclassify the stream, and
is handled by the governance group rather than by the owner.

Schema mechanics, including how a compatible change is registered and how an
incompatible one is staged, are separate from the notice question and live in
mcp:knowledge_page:kp_e9d7352a-d775-4f9d-b325-c49b8d57ca2c.","references":[{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_fb51a148-2fa5-4db6-a76b-217f70795075","type":"knowledge_page"},{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_e9d7352a-d775-4f9d-b325-c49b8d57ca2c","type":"knowledge_page"}]}}

{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_e9d7352a-d775-4f9d-b325-c49b8d57ca2c","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_e9d7352a-d775-4f9d-b325-c49b8d57ca2c","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Schema Registry Operations","body":"# Schema Registry Operations

A schema version is registered before a producer writes it, and the registry
refuses a version that is incompatible with the stream's declared compatibility
mode.

## Staging an incompatible version

An incompatible version is staged rather than registered: the new version is
written to a shadow subject, consumers are moved across one at a time, and the
subject is promoted once the last consumer reads the new version cleanly. The
staging mechanics say nothing about when the change may happen; that is the
change class's business.

## Rollback

A registered version is never deleted, only superseded. Rolling back means
registering the previous definition as a new version, so the history reads
forward and a consumer that pinned a version still resolves it."}}

Every consumer of a published stream registers a contract. The contract records
the consuming service, the schema version it reads, an owner who can be reached,
and whether the consumer is idempotent.

The registry is what an announcement is sent to. A consumer that never
registered is not announced to, which is the reason the registration is a
condition of read access rather than a courtesy.

Contracts are re-confirmed when a consumer changes the version it reads.
A contract that has not been confirmed for a year is flagged in the quarterly
review as a probable orphan; flagged contracts are confirmed or removed, never
left flagged."}}

platform channel, and the registry entry for the interface being changed. The

consumer onboarded after the announcement will still see. Who the mailing
reaches is decided by the contracts registered against the interface
(mcp:knowledge_page:kp_1d8c460d-54fe-4272-bf5b-755fb6cc4afe).

An announcement contains what is changing, the window it will be applied in, who
signed it off, and how a consumer says it is not ready. It does not contain a
justification: consumers act on the change, not on the reason for it.

How far ahead of the window an announcement has to go out is not a channel

## State

The state field takes one of five values: created, activated, moved, settled,
refunded. States are not ordered: a subscription can move several times between
activation and settlement, and a refund can follow a settlement by months.

## Money

Two money fields travel on each record, both integers in minor units, both in the
account's own currency. There is no converted amount on the record; conversion is
a reporting concern and is done against the rate table for the settlement date.

## Refund-only fields

The reason code and the original reference are populated only on refunded
records. Treating an absent reason code as "no reason given" therefore
misreports every non-refund record as a refund without a reason."}}

The general ledger extract is due nightly at 03:40 and by 06:00 on the first two
working days of a month, when the close batch runs ahead of it.

## Close periods

A close period runs to the last working day of the month. Records dated inside a
closed period are never restated in place; a correction is posted into the open
period with a reference back.

## Freeze

Platform changes that touch anything the ledger reads are frozen from the last
working day of the month to the second working day of the next. The freeze does
not stop an incident response, and a change applied during a freeze for incident
reasons is recorded as such."}}

2. Declare an expected throughput. The declaration sizes the partitions; a
   producer that exceeds its declaration by an order of magnitude is throttled
   rather than allowed to starve the others.
3. Wire a dead-letter destination. A producer with nowhere to put a rejected
   record will retry it forever.
4. Name an owner who can be paged.
5. Watch the first week. Most contract mismatches appear on the first weekend,
   when the traffic mix changes and fields that were always present stop being
   present.

The checklist covers putting a producer on a stream. It does not cover changing

{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_550d8b13-d702-47cf-9f09-80f21c6e7ee9","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_550d8b13-d702-47cf-9f09-80f21c6e7ee9","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Nightly Batch Window Calendar","body":"# Nightly Batch Window Calendar

The overnight schedule is divided into windows, each owned by one job family. A
job that overruns its window is not killed, but the window behind it starts late
and the delay accumulates across the night.

| Window | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| 22:00 - 23:15 | collector drain |
| 23:15 - 00:45 | raw exports |
| 00:45 - 02:00 | maintenance and vacuum |
| 02:00 - 04:00 | aggregation |
| 04:00 - 05:30 | reconciliation |

Moving a window is a scheduling change, not a job change: the request goes to the
platform group with the reason and the earliest night it can take effect. A move
that pushes any window past 05:30 needs the aggregation owner's agreement,

An escalation route is an ordered list of rungs. An incident starts at the first
rung and climbs one rung at a time; skipping a rung is allowed only when the
person on it is the one escalating.

## The routes

**Red route.** First rung: the owning team's shift lead. Second rung: the
platform duty manager. Third rung: the head of platform. Fourth rung: the
executive on call.

**Amber route.** First rung: the owning team's shift lead. **Second rung: the
platform duty manager.** Third rung: the head of platform.

**Standard route.** First rung: the owning team's shift lead. Second rung: the
owning team's manager, during working hours only.

## Timings

The routes above say who, and in what order. How long an incident may sit on a
rung before it climbs is not part of the route, because the same rung is worked
to different clocks on different routes; those clocks are held in
mcp:knowledge_page:kp_8883d7f9-4dfd-42d6-9691-f887a075c444.

Who is on shift on any given night is the rotation's business
(mcp:knowledge_page:kp_f7e100d4-816b-40b9-9d46-887e42ca8ea0), and the channel each rung is reached on is
listed in mcp:knowledge_page:kp_e4294a2c-a0e7-45c8-a9fb-3b97ce018e2a.","references":[{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_8883d7f9-4dfd-42d6-9691-f887a075c444","type":"knowledge_page"},{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_f7e100d4-816b-40b9-9d46-887e42ca8ea0","type":"knowledge_page"},{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_e4294a2c-a0e7-45c8-a9fb-3b97ce018e2a","type":"knowledge_page"}]}}

An incident is assigned a severity band when it is opened; opening one, and
what closing one takes, has its own mechanics (mcp:knowledge_page:kp_c0ba809a-7b02-4cac-9771-3b40c2682647).
The band is a statement about consequence, not about effort: a small defect
with an accounting consequence outranks a large one without.

## The bands

**Band A.** Customer-visible loss of service, or a defect that has already
produced an incorrect external figure. Notified immediately to the whole
platform group.

**Band B.** An internal control that has stopped proving what it exists to
prove, with no external figure yet affected. Notified to the owning team and to
the platform group's shift lead.

**Band C.** A degradation with a known workaround already in place.

**Band D.** A defect with no consequence before the next working day.

## Escalation

Each band follows a named escalation route, and the routes are held together in
mcp:knowledge_page:kp_36b25264-b9f1-464a-95b9-e3831ae06627 so a change to one is visible against the others.
Band A follows the red route, **band B follows the amber route**, bands C and D
follow the standard route.

What is said while an incident is open, and by whom, is not a band question
(mcp:knowledge_page:kp_1c337dbd-197b-4314-934b-411f802a9ff3).

# Change Plan — Adding a Field to the `billing-events` Stream

**Prepared for:** the owner of the `billing-events` stream
**Date prepared:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** executable as written, subject to the open items listed in §11

---

## 1. What this plan covers

Adding one new field to the records carried on the `billing-events` stream, from first proposal to the field being live and documented. It covers the approvals the change needs, the rules that constrain when it may be applied, the mechanics of registering the schema, and everything owed to the stream's consumers.

**What is settled before anything else:** `billing-events` is a **regulated-tier** stream (*Billing Events Stream Runbook*). The tier is not a property of the payload — it is a property of what downstream consumers are obliged to do with the data — and it is assigned by the data governance group, reviewed annually (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*).

**Every regulated-tier stream is governed by change class CC-3** (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*). That single fact fixes the two hardest constraints in this plan:

- **Sign-off is the data governance group's**, not the stream owner's and not the owning team's.
- **Consumers are owed 9 business days of advance notice** before the change is applied.

(*Change Class Reference*)

This holds regardless of how small or how compatible the field addition is. CC-2 ("additive", owning-team sign-off, two business days' notice) is the class a compatible addition would carry on an ordinary stream, but the regulated tier overrides it: the tier governs the stream, and the class follows the tier. **If the owner believes this change needs less notice than CC-3 requires, that is a request to reclassify the stream, and it is handled by the governance group rather than by the owner** (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*). Do not treat "it's only an added field" as a route to a lighter class.

---

## 2. Decisions to settle before the proposal is written

The proposal cannot be reviewed until these are answered. Several of them determine which execution path (§6) the change takes.

| Decision | Why it matters | Grounding |
|---|---|---|
| Field name, type, and whether it is required or optional | Determines whether the registry will accept the new version or force a staged rollout | *Schema Registry Operations* |
| Which of the five states populate it (`created`, `activated`, `moved`, `settled`, `refunded`) | The record already carries fields populated only on `refunded` records; a new conditionally-populated field joins that pattern and must be documented as such | *Billing Events Field Guide* |
| **The meaning of the field's absence** | This is the stream's known failure mode. Reason code and original reference are populated only on refunds, and "treating an absent reason code as *no reason given* misreports every non-refund record as a refund without a reason." A new field with undocumented absence semantics repeats that defect | *Billing Events Field Guide* |
| If the field is a money field: units and currency | Both existing money fields are integers in minor units in the account's own currency, with no converted amount on the record — conversion is a reporting concern done against the rate table for the settlement date. A new money field should follow this convention or explicitly state why it does not | *Billing Events Field Guide* |
| Which of the three producing services will populate it, and what the other producers write in its place | All three producers write to this stream; a field only one of them populates is a field consumers will see as intermittently absent | *Billing Events Stream Runbook* |
| The value written for records produced before the change | Records already in the 14-day retention window will not carry the field, and they remain replayable (§8) | *Billing Events Stream Runbook*, *Billing Events Replay Guide* |

---

## 3. Approvals required

| Approval | Who gives it | When | Grounding |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Change sign-off (CC-3)** | The data governance group | Before the announcement goes out — the announcement must name who signed it off | *Change Class Reference*, *Change Announcement Channels* |
| **Producer attestation** | The named owner of *each* producing service | After the change, per producer: an attestation that the records that service writes are complete | *Regulated Tier Operating Rules* |
| **Egress approval — conditional** | The data governance group | Before the field is live, *if* any route carrying `billing-events` data writes to a destination the platform does not operate | *Data Egress Approval Policy* |
| **Emergency sign-off — only on the CC-5 path** | The platform duty manager | Only if §10 applies | *Change Class Reference*, *Duty Manager Rota* |

Two notes on approvals:

- **Egress.** Any route writing platform data to a destination the platform does not operate is an egress, whether it runs once or nightly, and needs a named recipient, a stated purpose and an end date. Approval sits with the data governance group, and every approved route records per run what it sent and how much. **The available material does not record which — if any — `billing-events` consumer routes are egress routes.** Before the field is live, the owner must establish from the contract registry whether any registered consumer forwards records off-platform; if one does, whether the new field's content falls inside that route's approved purpose is a governance question, not the stream owner's call.
- **Reclassification.** Not an approval on the happy path, but the only legitimate route to a shorter notice period. It goes to the governance group.

---

## 4. Consumer discovery — do this before the announcement

The **consumer contract registry** is the list the announcement is sent to. Each contract records the consuming service, the schema version it reads, an owner who can be reached, and whether the consumer is idempotent. **A consumer that never registered is not announced to — which is why registration is a condition of read access rather than a courtesy** (*Consumer Contract Registry*).

Steps:

1. Pull every contract registered against `billing-events`. This is the announcement distribution list and the authoritative consumer set.
2. Note which contracts are **flagged as probable orphans** — a contract not confirmed for a year is flagged in the quarterly review, and flagged contracts are confirmed or removed, never left flagged (*Consumer Contract Registry*). Do not announce into an unresolved flag; get it confirmed or removed first, so the notice period is not spent waiting on a contract nobody owns.
3. Note which contracts are marked **not idempotent**. These matter for replay (§8), not for the field addition itself.
4. Note the **schema version each consumer has pinned**. This is the input to the staged-rollout path in §6b, and it tells you how many distinct versions are in live use.

**A judgment call worth stating plainly:** the *Stream Deprecation Runbook* identifies consumers from the contract registry **and from the last ninety days of read activity**, on the reasoning that a consumer reading monthly does not appear in a week of logs. That rule is written for deprecation, not for a field addition, and the material does not extend it to schema changes. It is nonetheless the only recorded way to find a reader the registry has missed. Recommended: run the 90-day read-activity check anyway and reconcile it against the registry. Any reader found in the logs but absent from the registry is an access-control defect on a regulated-tier stream and should be raised with governance regardless of this change.

---

## 5. The announcement — what is owed, where, and when

**Timing.** The announcement is the event the 9 business days are counted from. Nothing that follows it may start the clock again, so the announcement must be complete and correct when it goes out.

**Where it goes.** To three places at once (*Change Announcement Channels*):

1. The platform mailing list — reaching the owners recorded on the registered contracts.
2. The platform channel.
3. **The registry entry for `billing-events`** — this is the **authoritative** channel, because it is the only one a consumer onboarded *after* the announcement will still see.

**What it must contain** (*Change Announcement Channels*):

- What is changing — the field name, type, which records will carry it, and what its absence means.
- The window it will be applied in.
- Who signed it off — the data governance group, named.
- How a consumer says it is not ready.

**What it must not contain:** a justification. *"Consumers act on the change, not on the reason for it."* Keep the business rationale in the proposal to governance, out of the announcement.

---

## 6. Schema registry mechanics

**The governing rule: a schema version is registered before a producer writes it, and the registry refuses a version that is incompatible with the stream's declared compatibility mode** (*Schema Registry Operations*).

**The material does not record `billing-events`' declared compatibility mode, and it does not state whether an added field is compatible under that mode.** The owner must read the mode off the registry before choosing a path. Both paths are given below; the registry itself will decide which one applies when the version is submitted.

### 6a. If the new version is compatible

1. Register the new schema version.
2. Confirm the registration resolved cleanly for consumers pinned to prior versions.
3. Roll the producers forward to write the field (§7).

### 6b. If the new version is incompatible (e.g. a required field with no default)

An incompatible version is **staged, not registered** (*Schema Registry Operations*):

1. Write the new version to a **shadow subject**.
2. **Move consumers across one at a time.** Each move is a change of the version that consumer reads, which requires that consumer's contract to be re-confirmed (*Consumer Contract Registry*).
3. **Promote the subject once the last consumer reads the new version cleanly.** Not before.

Two things the material is explicit about, and one it is silent on:

- The staging mechanics **say nothing about when the change may happen — that is the change class's business.** Staging does not shorten or replace the 9 business days' notice.
- Promotion is gated on the *last* consumer, so a single unmoved consumer holds the change open indefinitely.
- **The material does not say how long a shadow subject may run, nor what happens if a consumer will not move.** The parallel-running-until-the-last-consumer-moves guarantee is written for CC-4 (breaking), not CC-3. If a consumer refuses or cannot move, that is a question for governance — see §11.

### 6c. Rollback (either path)

**A registered version is never deleted, only superseded.** Rolling back means **registering the previous definition as a new version**, so the history reads forward and a consumer that pinned a version still resolves it (*Schema Registry Operations*). Write the rollback version's definition before the change window opens, so rolling back is a registration and not an authoring exercise under pressure.

---

## 7. Producer rollout

The *Stream Onboarding Checklist* explicitly **does not cover this**: *"The checklist covers putting a producer on a stream. It does not cover changing what the stream carries."* Only the items below are grounded; they are drawn from the regulated-tier rules and from the checklist's stated purposes where those clearly still apply.

1. **Do not write the field before the version carrying it is registered or staged.** The registry gate is stated as "registered before a producer writes it." A producer emitting an unregistered field risks records being rejected — and a producer with nowhere to put a rejected record retries it forever, which is why each producer has a **dead-letter destination**. Confirm each producer's dead-letter destination is wired and being watched across the change.
2. **Roll producers in a known order and record it.** Until all three have rolled, the field will be present on some records and absent on others; that interval must be documented in the announcement's "what is changing" text and in the field guide (§9).
3. **Producer attestation.** Each producing service's named owner attests, *after any change*, that the records it writes are complete (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*). Collect all three attestations. This is a tier obligation, not a formality — an unattested producer on a regulated stream is an open compliance item.
4. **Throughput.** Producers declare an expected throughput, and the declaration sizes the partitions; a producer exceeding its declaration by an order of magnitude is throttled (*Stream Onboarding Checklist*). **The material does not say whether adding a field to existing records requires re-declaring throughput.** A single added field is very unlikely to move volume by an order of magnitude, so no re-declaration is planned here — flagged so the owner can overrule it if the field is large.
5. **Watch the first week.** The checklist's reasoning applies directly to this change: *"Most contract mismatches appear on the first weekend, when the traffic mix changes and fields that were always present stop being present."* A conditionally-populated new field is exactly that shape. Plan an explicit first-weekend check.

---

## 8. Replay and the records already in the window

The stream retains **fourteen days** of replayable records — a regulated-tier retention floor, held regardless of the volume it implies (*Billing Events Stream Runbook*, *Regulated Tier Operating Rules*).

Consequences the consumers are owed in writing:

- **For fourteen days after the change, the replay window straddles the change boundary.** Records written before the change do not carry the field and cannot be made to: *"A replay is not a repair: a record that was never written cannot be replayed"* (*Billing Events Replay Guide*). A consumer replaying across the boundary sees the field present on the newer part and absent on the older part.
- If a replay is needed during or after the change: **choose the offset by timestamp, not by count** — counting back is wrong whenever a producer has been backfilling, and a producer rollout is exactly that situation.
- **Pause the consumers that are not idempotent** for the duration of the replay; the contract registry says which those are. A paused consumer resumes from its own committed offset, so nothing is lost by pausing.
- **Confirm any replay afterwards** by comparing the record count in the replayed window against the count the consumer processed. *"A replay that is not confirmed is a replay nobody can distinguish from a no-op."*

**Backfilling the field into existing records is not available.** The material offers no mechanism to add a field to records already written; replay redelivers what is held, it does not rewrite it. If consumers need the field for historical records, that is a separate piece of work and is out of this plan's scope.

---

## 9. Documentation owed after the change

- **Registry entry for `billing-events`** — the authoritative announcement channel; it must reflect the new version and the applied change, since it is the only channel a later-onboarded consumer will see.
- **Billing Events Field Guide** — the page that carries field-by-field meaning. Add the new field: its meaning, its type and units, which of the five states populate it, and **what its absence means**. The field guide's own worked example of absence semantics going wrong (reason code) is the reason this is mandatory rather than nice-to-have.
- **Billing Events Stream Runbook** — no change required by the field itself; it points at the field guide for field meanings. Update only if the change alters producers or tiering, which it should not.
- **Consumer contracts** — contracts are re-confirmed when a consumer changes the version it reads (*Consumer Contract Registry*). Every consumer that moves to the new version re-confirms its contract. On the staged path (§6b) this happens consumer by consumer.

---

## 10. When the change may be applied

Three constraints stack. All must be satisfied.

### 10a. Notice — 9 business days

Counted **in business days from the announcement to the change window opening, excluding the announcement day itself** (*Change Class Reference*).

### 10b. The ledger close freeze

**Platform changes that touch anything the ledger reads are frozen from the last working day of the month to the second working day of the next month** (*Ledger Close Calendar*).

**This change falls inside that freeze scope.** The chain: every finance-facing report consumes `billing-events` directly or through the settled-invoice view (*Billing Events Stream Runbook*), and the nightly `ledger-reconcile` job compares the settled-invoice view against the general ledger extract (*Ledger Reconcile Job Runbook*). A change to what `billing-events` carries therefore touches what the ledger reads. This is a reading of the rule rather than a sentence in it — the freeze rule does not name `billing-events` — so confirm it with governance at sign-off. Plan on the freeze applying.

Also note: **records dated inside a closed period are never restated in place; a correction is posted into the open period with a reference back** (*Ledger Close Calendar*). This is a further reason not to attempt any historical treatment of the new field.

### 10c. Notice ending inside a freeze

**A notice period that would end inside a change freeze runs to the first business day after the freeze lifts** (*Change Class Reference*). The notice is not shortened and the announcement is not reissued; the window simply opens later.

### 10d. Worked example from today

Assuming an announcement on **Monday 2026-08-10**, and assuming no public holidays (the available material records no holiday calendar — verify against the organisation's before committing dates):

- Business days counted, excluding the announcement day: Tue 11, Wed 12, Thu 13, Fri 14, Mon 17, Tue 18, Wed 19, Thu 20, **Fri 21 Aug — the ninth**.
- **Earliest change window: Monday 2026-08-24.** (A less conservative reading of "counted to the window opening" would allow Fri 21 Aug. The rule does not disambiguate; Mon 24 Aug is the safe reading and costs one business day.)
- **August close freeze:** last working day of August is **Mon 31 Aug**; the first two working days of September are Tue 1 and Wed 2 Sep. **Freeze runs Mon 31 Aug – Wed 2 Sep inclusive; changes resume Thu 3 Sep.**
- A window in the week of **Mon 24 – Fri 28 Aug** is clear of the freeze. If the change slips past Fri 28 Aug, the next available date is **Thu 3 Sep**.

### 10e. Time of day

The *Nightly Batch Window Calendar* divides the overnight schedule into windows owned by job families (collector drain 22:00–23:15, raw exports 23:15–00:45, maintenance and vacuum 00:45–02:00, aggregation 02:00–04:00, reconciliation 04:00–05:30). **These are job windows, and the material does not state that a stream schema change must be applied inside one of them, nor which one would own it.** Nothing here fixes a time of day for this change. Propose a time to governance, and — as a matter of judgment, not of recorded rule — avoid landing it mid-reconciliation (04:00–05:30), since reconciliation reads the settled-invoice view fed by this stream.

## 11. If something goes wrong

- **Anyone may open an incident, and the bias is deliberate:** *"Opening one costs almost nothing and not opening one costs the timeline."* An incident needs a one-line statement of what is wrong, the system it is wrong in, and who opened it; everything else is filled in as it is learned (*Opening and Closing an Incident*).
- **Band assignment is about consequence, not effort** — *"a small defect with an accounting consequence outranks a large one without"* (*Incident Severity Bands*). For this change, the realistic bands:
  - **Band A** if the change has already produced an incorrect external figure. Notified immediately to the whole platform group; follows the **red route** (shift lead → duty manager → head of platform → executive on call).
  - **Band B** if an internal control has stopped proving what it exists to prove with no external figure yet affected. Notified to the owning team and the platform group's shift lead; follows the **amber route** (shift lead → duty manager → head of platform).
- **The specific tripwire to watch after this change:** `ledger-reconcile` **failures on three consecutive nights open a band B incident**, because at that point the reconciliation has not been proved for a full accounting period (*Ledger Reconcile Job Runbook*). Watch the reconcile for at least three nights after the field goes live. Note the distinction the platform insists on: a **break** is one discrepancy the reconciliation *writes*; a **failure** is the job being unable to complete. They are worked by different people on different clocks (*Platform Glossary*).
- **Closing** an incident needs evidence the condition has gone, not an absence of further reports; for a scheduled job that means **a clean scheduled run**. A manual reconcile run does not close an incident (*Ledger Reconcile Job Runbook*, *Opening and Closing an Incident*). An incident is never deleted; one opened by mistake is closed as such.
- **Rollback** is §6c: register the previous definition as a new version. Never delete.
- **The freeze does not stop an incident response**, and a change applied during a freeze for incident reasons is recorded as such (*Ledger Close Calendar*).

### The CC-5 emergency path — and when it does *not* apply

**CC-5 is a change applied ahead of its notice because leaving the defect in place is worse.** Sign-off is the **duty manager's** (the role rotates monthly among the platform leads; a duty manager who will be unreachable names a standing delegate who *holds* the role — there is never a state with two holders or none). **The notice is reconstructed afterwards, with the reason recorded** (*Change Class Reference*, *Duty Manager Rota*).

CC-5 is not a route for delivering this field faster. It exists for a defect. Adding a new field is not a defect being left in place, so on the plan as written, **CC-3 applies and CC-5 does not**. CC-5 becomes relevant only if this change itself introduces a defect that must be corrected ahead of notice.

## 13. Where the available material is silent

These are gaps, not omissions from the plan. Each needs an answer from the governance group or the registry before or during execution; none is invented here.

1. **The membership and contact route of the data governance group.** The group is named as the sign-off authority for CC-3, regulated-tier assignment, and egress approval, but the material does not say who sits on it or how a proposal reaches it. **There is no recorded intake path or template for a CC-3 proposal.**
2. **`billing-events`' declared compatibility mode**, and therefore whether the specific field being added is compatible. This decides §6a vs §6b and is knowable only from the registry.
3. **What happens when a consumer says it is not ready.** The announcement must tell consumers how to say it, but the material does not say what that does — whether it delays the window, or is advisory. Parallel running until the last consumer has moved is specified for CC-4 (breaking), not CC-3; the staged path's "promote once the last consumer reads cleanly" is the nearest equivalent and applies only when the version is incompatible.
4. **How long a staged shadow subject may run**, and what happens to a consumer that will not move.
5. **The time of day / window a stream schema change is applied in.** The nightly batch calendar covers job families, not schema changes, and no window owns this.
6. **Whether a public holiday falls in the notice period.** Notice is counted in business days and the freeze in working days, but no holiday calendar is recorded. §10d assumes none.
7. **Whether the freeze rule covers this change.** §10b is a reading of "anything the ledger reads" via the settled-invoice view, not an explicit statement. Confirm at sign-off.
8. **Whether a field addition requires re-declaring producer throughput.** Assumed not, on the order-of-magnitude threshold; flagged.
9. **Which, if any, `billing-events` consumer routes are egress routes** under the egress policy.
10. **Whether the annual regulated-tier review or the quarterly access review falls inside the change window.** Both are recurring obligations on this stream; the material gives no dates for either.
